extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, policymakers, and scholars interested in limits of government and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical criteria about when and how government should intervene in social affairs (especially education, local administration, and marriage/reproduction), including instruments of enforcement, limits on content-control, and the proper balance between centralization and local autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to require and compel education
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should require and compel the education, up to a certain standard, of every human being who is born its citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The father's duty to provide education is widely recognised, but if parents fail the State ought to see it fulfilled, at the charge, as far as possible, of the parent; bringing a child into existence without fair prospect of being able to provide food and instruction is a moral crime against offspring and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish enforcement of education from State direction of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of education by the State is not the same as the State's taking upon itself to direct that education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections to State education generally apply to the State directing education (which risks moulding people alike), not to enforcing that parents ensure education. A State education, if it exists, should be one among many competing experiments rather than the sole model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer compulsory requirement with voluntary provision and State aid
rubrics_metrics.description: The government might require for every child a good education but leave to parents to obtain it where and how they please, while helping to pay school fees for poorer classes and bearing expenses for those with no one else to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine a law rendering education compulsory with State aid to those unable to defray the expense; voluntary provision preserves diversity while enforcement secures minimum standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public examinations as the instrument for enforcing compulsory education
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument for enforcing the law could be no other than public examinations, extending to all children and beginning at an early age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An age might be fixed for initial examination (e.g., ability to read); annual renewal with extending subjects; a father whose child proves unable may be subjected to a moderate fine and the child put to school at his expense; examinations make acquisition and retention of a minimum of general knowledge virtually compulsory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define a minimum compulsory curriculum and keep higher examinations voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a certain minimum of general knowledge made virtually compulsory; beyond that minimum there should be voluntary examinations of all subjects at which those meeting a proficiency standard might claim a certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher branches of knowledge should be voluntary to avoid giving governments dangerous powers to exclude people from professions for alleged deficiency of qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit examination content to facts and positive science; avoid testing disputed opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the State from improperly influencing opinion, the knowledge required for passing an examination (beyond merely instrumental parts such as languages) should be confined to facts and positive science exclusively; examinations on religion, politics, or other disputed topics should not turn on the truth or falsehood of opinions but on the matter of fact that such an opinion is held on such grounds by such authors, schools, or churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach prevents the State from biasing citizens' conclusions while allowing certification that a person possesses knowledge relevant to forming worth-attending conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow examination without compulsion of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: A student (e.g., an atheist) may be examined in the evidences of a religion provided he is not required to profess belief in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations may test knowledge of arguments and authors without coercing assent or religious profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates should not confer special legal or professional advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees or other public certificates of scientific or professional acquirements should be given to all who present themselves for examination and stand the test; but such certificates should confer no advantage over competitors other than the weight attached by public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents governments from using certification as a gatekeeping tool to exclude people from professions; maintains voluntary and open professional access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should abstain when individuals can better perform the function
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to government interference: when the thing to be done is likely to be better done by individuals than by the government — those personally interested are best qualified to conduct business and decide how it shall be conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle condemns many interferences of legislature or officers with ordinary industry; where individuals can act, government should generally refrain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of local and voluntary institutions for civic development
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when individuals may not do a thing so well on average as government officers, it is desirable that it be done by them as a means of mental education — strengthening active faculties, judgment, and knowledge of joint interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal recommendation for jury trial (in non-political cases), free and popular local and municipal institutions, and voluntary associations; these create habits and powers necessary for maintaining a free constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: State's role as central depository and diffuser of experience, not sole operator
rubrics_metrics.description: What the State can usefully do is to make itself a central depository, active circulator, and diffuser of the experience resulting from many trials; enabling each experimenter to benefit by others' experiments instead of tolerating no experiments but its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central organ should concentrate information and experience from localities and foreign analogues and make that knowledge available; its actual power should be limited to compelling local officers to obey laws laid down for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency; centralize information
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical principle and standard for testing arrangements is: the greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency; but the greatest possible centralization of information, and diffusion of it from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by having minute local divisions of business managed by local officers while a central superintendence concentrates information and advises, yet limits its power to enforcing compliance with general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expanding government functions that unduly increase its power and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief reason for restricting government interference is the great evil of adding unnecessarily to its power: every function superadded diffuses its influence and converts the active and ambitious part of the public into hangers-on of the government or a party aiming to become the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of roads, railways, banks, universities, charities, municipal corporations, etc., under government, and government-paid employees seeking advancement through the state, risks creating a bureaucracy that dominates the nation and resists reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit administrative power; local officers responsible to constituencies and law
rubrics_metrics.description: Local officers should be chosen by the localities and, except for obeying laws, left to their own judgment under responsibility to their constituents; the central administrative authority should watch execution and, if rules are not carried into effect, appeal to tribunals or constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central organ's duty is to make knowledge acquired in one place available for others and to compel obedience to laws, but actual coercive powers beyond this should be sparingly used and limited to cases of first-rate national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should inform, advise, and stimulate rather than substitute its activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A government cannot have too much of the activity which aids and stimulates individual exertion and development; the mischief begins when it substitutes its own activity for that of individuals, doing their work instead of informing, advising, or denouncing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect the worth of the State by fostering individual mental expansion; avoid creating dependency that shrinks citizens' capacities and leaves only a skilled administrative machine without vital power.

rubrics_metrics.name: State regulation of marriage/reproduction permissible to prevent social harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws which forbid marriage unless the parties can show that they have the means of supporting a family do not exceed the legitimate powers of the State; producing children beyond a small number in an over-populated country, with the effect of reducing the reward of labour by competition, is a serious offence against others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether such laws are expedient depends on local circumstances and feelings, but they are defensible as interferences to prohibit acts injurious to others and may be accompanied by social stigma even if legal punishment is not added.
